name: Sleeping Beauty diet

card.summary: A fringe weight-loss practice of staying asleep or sedated for long stretches so as to eat less, pursued to get a leaner look.
card.note: Sedative-induced prolonged sleep is associated with documented deaths in historical deep sleep therapy.

quick.overview:
The Sleeping Beauty diet is a fringe idea in which a person uses sedatives to sleep for much of the day, so that fewer hours are spent awake and eating. Those who try it are seeking weight loss for a slimmer appearance.

No clinical studies test it as a diet. Its closest medical relative, prolonged sedation or deep sleep therapy, was used psychiatrically in the 20th century and has been linked to deaths and severe memory loss.
quick.how: Descriptions of the practice involve extended sedation to reduce waking hours; the specifics are not given here. Discussion appears mostly in anecdote and in media coverage rather than in structured protocols.
quick.risks: Prolonged unconsciousness carried deaths in deep sleep therapy, including 25 patient deaths at one Sydney hospital across the 1960s and 70s, and severe memory loss was reported. Sedatives carry dependence and overdose risks. Anyone considering extreme weight loss methods is advised by clinicians to speak to a doctor.

lead: The Sleeping Beauty diet is a practice, described in popular media and some forums, of using sedation to sleep for long periods in order to eat less and lose weight. People turn to it to slim down and so change how they look.

It resembles deep sleep therapy, a discredited psychiatric treatment in which drugs kept patients unconscious for days or weeks; obesity was among the conditions it was prescribed for [1]. No published trial has tested sedation-induced sleep as a weight-loss method.

angle.text: Adherents claim that spending most of the day asleep cuts food intake and thus body weight. The claim is untested in trials.

paras: Sleep therapy with sedatives was tried by Scottish psychiatrist Neil Macleod around 1900, with a patient death; Swiss psychiatrist Jakob Klaesi popularised barbiturate-induced prolonged sleep in the early 1920s, mostly for schizophrenia [1]. At Chelmsford Private Hospital in New South Wales, Harry Bailey used it from 1962 to 1979 for conditions including obesity, and 25 patients died, leading to a Royal Commission [1].
Documented harms of prolonged sedation include deaths and severe memory loss; psychiatrist William Sargant wrote that patients often did not know how long they had slept [1].
No studies found on the Sleeping Beauty diet itself. Historical records of prolonged sleep therapy describe obesity as one of many conditions treated, without trial data on weight outcomes [1].

timeline.event: Neil Macleod tries sleep induction with sodium bromide [1]
Jakob Klaesi popularises barbiturate sleep therapy [1]
Chelmsford Hospital, Sydney, deep sleep therapy practised; 25 deaths [1]
